To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
overexpression of antioxidant enzymes in the hippocampus in middle age results in an altered redox state, impaired cognition, and altered synaptic plastic.

overexpression of superoxide-dismutase 1 ( SOD1 ) in the hippocampus in middle-aged rats results in age-dependent impairment in cognition, decreased synaptic plasticity, and altered redox environment.
overexpression of SOD1 in the hippocampus in middle-aged rats results in impaired learning, decreased NMDA receptor function, and decreased glutathione redox potential.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding how oxidative stress affects the brain.
the role of oxidative and redox processes in the aging brain and their role in age-related neurodegeneration and cognitive dysfunction.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the effects of Sod1 on NMDA receptor function are mediated via a shift in the neuronal redox environment.
SOD1 over-expression in middle age results in an increase in hydrogen peroxide and a decrease in glutathione, which results in a decrease in synaptic plasticity.
the overexpression of SOD1 in the hippocampus in middle-aged rats results in impaired cognition and altered hippocampal synaptic function that is mediated by a redox imbalance.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the effects of Sod1 overexpression on learning and synaptic function in middle-aged rats are mediated by a shift in the cellular redox environment and are not due to an altered redox status of the NMDAR.
overexpression of SOD1 alone or SOD1 +CAT in the middle-aged brain causes an age-dependent impairment in cognition and synaptic plasticity.

SOD1 over-expression is a model for studying age-related cognitive deficits and that SOD1 is not the primary source of oxidative stress and that the redox environment may be a critical factor in the age-related decline in synaptic function and cognition.
The main takeaway from our work is that

overexpression of SOD1 in middle-aged rats causes a decrease in glutathione and NMDAR function, but that the effect is rescued when catalase is co-expressed suggesting the effects are mediated by excess hydrogenperoxide.

the overexpression of superoxide in the hippocampus in middle-aged rats results in an increase in hydrogen peroxide that is responsible for the decrease in glutathione peroxides, glutathione, NMDA receptor-mediated synaptic transmission, and learning.

the overexpression of SOD1 in the middle-aged rat hippocampus is sufficient to alter synaptic plasticity and learning, and that these effects are mediated, at least in part, by an altered redox state.
